title: What is known about 1RB0RE_1LC0RA_1LA1LD_1LC1LF_0LC0LB_1LE---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RE_1LC0RA_1LA1LD_1LC1LF_0LC0LB_1LE---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and Collatz-like. The run is a sequence of phases M → 8M/3 + c (proved in Lean for the empty tail and the tail [6]); the residue M mod 3 edits a small stack of blocks, and the machine halts exactly when that stack reaches one of a few shapes with two adjacent blocks 0 1 1. 30,000 phases from blank tape (far past 1025000 steps) do not halt.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 69,315 cells have been visited and 35,991 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The rounds of a phase
claims.text: From PS(M, T) = 0^inf F> 0 1^M T, five ones become a wall (10)^5; each round trip of the head then eats three ones and adds four 10 to the wall (6k + 39 steps for a wall of k pairs); at the end, state C turns every 10 of the wall into 11. Each for every k, m and any tape beyond.

claims.title: Whole phases on the empty tail and the tail [6]
claims.text: For every j: PS(3j+5, []) → PS(8j+17, []), PS(3j+6, []) → PS(8j+19, []), PS(3j+7, []) → PS(8j+13, [6]), PS(3j+5, [6]) → PS(8j+23, []), PS(3j+6, [6]) → PS(8j+35, []), PS(3j+7, [6]) → PS(8j+17, [1, 1, 3]). The rounds are chained by induction.

claims.title: The phase map on every tail
claims.text: For any tail, the next phase start is found by running the machine on three small M of the same residue mod 3 and extrapolating linearly (slope 8/3 and the same new tail at all three, checked each time). This agrees with the real machine on the first nine phases from blank tape (to step 1.19·10<sup>9</sup>). The tail changes by simple push/pop rules, and it halts exactly on a few tails such as [2, 2] with M ≡ 1 mod 3.

claims.title: No halt in 30,000 phases
claims.text: Iterating the phase map from PS(9, []) for 30,000 phases (assuming the linear extrapolation, checked as above): no halt; the tail stays at most 26 cells and 9 blocks; M then has about 12,800 digits, so this covers far more than 10<sup>25000</sup> steps.

claims.title: Halting needs a long, specific run of residues
claims.text: With the residues M mod 3 chosen freely, a halting tail can be reached from [], so nothing about the tail alone rules halting out; but it takes 108 phases of the right residues, and with residues taken as random, 3·10<sup>6</sup> phases had no halt.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts exactly if the residues of M mod 3 along the orbit of the phase map ever build a halting tail: a Collatz-like question.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, and the question is a cousin of the Collatz problem. Each phase, the machine turns a block of M ones into a wall and back into about 8M/3 ones. What M is mod 3 decides what happens to a short stack of blocks at the right end of the tape, and the machine stops only if that stack ever takes one rare shape.

facts.text: Each phase multiplies the block of ones by about 8/3; proved in Lean for every M on the two commonest tails, in all six cases.
No halt from blank tape, far past 10<sup>25000</sup> steps.
The shortest run of chosen residues that builds a halting stack.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.51). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 69,315 cells (55,399 left of the start, 15 right), with a density of 1s of 0.519.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A phase: ones to wall and back
html: A phase starts with the head in state F just left of a block of M ones, 0^inf F> 0 1^M T, where T is the tail. Five ones become a wall (10)^5. Then, every round trip of the head across the wall eats three more ones at the wall's right end and adds four 10 pairs at its left end, so the tape keeps growing to the left. When fewer than three ones are left, the head meets the tail, changes it, and runs left turning each 10 into 11. The wall had about 4M/3 pairs, so the next block has about 8M/3 ones.

M mod 3tail []tail [6]
2(8M + 11)/3, tail [](8M + 29)/3, tail []
0(8M + 9)/3, tail [](8M + 57)/3, tail []
1(8M − 17)/3, tail [6](8M − 5)/3, tail [1, 1, 3]
All six cases are proved in Lean for every M. A phase costs about 4M2/3 steps, which is why the left side grows like a square root.

sections.heading: The stack beside the block
html: The tail is a list of blocks 0 1^t, written [t1, t2, …]. Which residue M has decides what the end of the phase does to it. With M ≡ 2 the first block is popped. With M ≡ 1 the first long block is counted down by three and two 1-blocks are pushed in front ([6] → [1, 1, 3]), and a tail of L ones turns into one block [2L + 6]. With M ≡ 0 the tail is mostly cleared.

The machine halts in only a few of these cases, all with two adjacent blocks of two ones: [2, 2] with M ≡ 1, [2, 2, 2] with M ≡ 0 or 1, [5, 2, 2] with M ≡ 0, and a few more. Building such a stack needs a long run of residues in a specific order. If the residues are chosen freely, 108 phases are enough. Along the real orbit they never lined up in 30,000 phases.

sections.heading: A Collatz-like question
html: Halting is now a question about the numbers M0 = 9, M1 = 27, M2 = 75, … and their residues mod 3. Each M is about 8/3 of the last, plus a constant that depends on the stack. Questions like this are believed to be out of reach of current methods. If the residues behave like coin flips, halting is very unlikely in any time we could simulate.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: A block of M ones is turned into a wall and back each phase, M -> about 8M/3; the residue M mod 3 pushes, pops and edits a small stack of blocks beside it, and the machine halts only if that stack ever holds two adjacent blocks of two ones in the right residue.
